hints: Think about what happens in each process, does forming a lattice from gaseous ions or forming water from acid plus alkali release energy or take it in?
walkthrough:
Picture lattice formation**
Imagine separate gaseous ions coming together to build a solid lattice. Opposite charges attract strongly, bonds form, and energy is released to the surroundings. Forming bonds is always exothermic, so $\Delta H^{\ominus}_{latt}$ is always negative.

Picture neutralisation**
Neutralisation is essentially $\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{OH}^{-}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}\text{O}(\text{l})$. You are forming a covalent O-H bond to make water, which releases energy. That is why $\Delta H^{\ominus}_{neut}$ is always negative, about $-57$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ for strong acid plus strong base.
Final answer: lattice energy: always negative (✓); enthalpy change of neutralisation: always negative (✓).

hints: Recall that every standard enthalpy definition must state the amount dissolved and the amount of solvent to prevent further dilution enthalpy.
walkthrough:
Build the precise definition**
You need three pieces. The amount of solute is $1$ mole. The solvent is water, and you use so much water that adding more causes no further heat change. That is called infinite water, giving a dilute solution. Put together: $\text{solute(s)} + \text{aq} \rightarrow \text{solution(aq)}$, $\Delta H^{\ominus}_{sol}$.
Final answer: The energy change when 1 mole of solute is dissolved in an infinite amount of water to form a dilute solution under standard conditions.

hints: Sketch a Hess cycle with $\text{K}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}(\text{s})$ at the top, elements $3\text{K(s)} + \text{P(s)} + 2\text{O}_{2}(\text{g})$ at the bottom left, and aqueous ions $3\text{K}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{PO}_{4}^{3-}(\text{aq})$ at the bottom right.
Identify which route goes via $\Delta H^{\ominus}_{f}$ of the solid and which route goes via the two given aqueous ion formation enthalpies to reach the same dissolved products.
Remember the formula $\text{K}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ produces three $\text{K}^{+}$ ions, so one of the given values must be multiplied by 3 before applying Hess law.
walkthrough:
Set up the Hess cycle in your head**
Start from elements: $3\text{K(s)} + \text{P(s)} + 2\text{O}_{2}(\text{g})$. One arrow goes up to $\text{K}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}(\text{s})$ with $\Delta H^{\ominus}_{f} = -2035$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. The other route goes to aqueous ions: $3\text{K}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{PO}_{4}^{3-}(\text{aq})$. Then $\text{K}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}(\text{s}) \rightarrow$ aqueous ions is the $\Delta H^{\ominus}_{sol}$ you want.

Write the aqueous ion route correctly**
For phosphate: $\text{P(s)} + 2\text{O}_{2}(\text{g}) + 3\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{PO}_{4}^{3-}(\text{aq})$, $\Delta H^{\ominus} = -1284$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. For potassium: $\text{K(s)} \rightarrow \text{K}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{e}^{-}$, $\Delta H^{\ominus} = -251$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, but you need $3$ moles of $\text{K}$, so $3 \times (-251)$. The electrons cancel: $3\text{e}^{-}$ produced and $3\text{e}^{-}$ consumed.

Apply Hess law and calculate**
By Hess, formation enthalpy plus solution enthalpy equals the aqueous route:
$$\Delta H^{\ominus}_{f} + \Delta H^{\ominus}_{sol} = 3(-251) + (-1284)$$
Rearrange:
$$\Delta H^{\ominus}_{sol} = [3 \times (-251) + (-1284)] - (-2035)$$
$$\Delta H^{\ominus}_{sol} = -753 -1284 + 2035 = -2 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

hints: Compare the ions present, $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ versus $\text{K}^{+}$ with the same anion $\text{Br}^{-}$, focusing on charge and size.
Link greater charge density to the strength of electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions when the lattice forms.
walkthrough:
Compare the cations**
Both lattices contain $\text{Br}^{-}$, so the difference must come from the cation. $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ carries a $2+$ charge while $\text{K}^{+}$ carries only $1+$. They are in a similar period with similar small sizes, so $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ has a much higher charge density.

Link charge to lattice energy**
Lattice energy is the energy released when gaseous ions pack into a solid: $\text{Ca}^{2+}(\text{g}) + 2\text{Br}^{-}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{CaBr}_{2}(\text{s})$. Higher charge means stronger electrostatic attraction between $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Br}^{-}$. More energy is released, so $\Delta H^{\ominus}_{latt}$ is more negative, $-2176$ compared with $-679$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Final answer: $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ has a higher charge / greater charge density than $\text{K}^{+}$.
Stronger electrostatic attraction between $\text{Br}^{-}$ and $\text{Ca}^{2+}$, so more energy released on lattice formation.

hints: Recall how $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ combines enthalpy, temperature in kelvin, and entropy into one expression for feasibility.
walkthrough:
State the Gibbs relationship**
Free energy balances enthalpy against the entropy term scaled by absolute temperature:
$$\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$$
$T$ must be in $\text{K}$, $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ in $\text{kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$ for consistent units.
Final answer: $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$.

hints: Look at the graph, $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ falls as $T$ rises, and compare with the form $y = c - m x$ where gradient $= -\Delta S^{\ominus}$.
walkthrough:
Read the slope to find the sign of entropy**
The plot of $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ against $T$ is a straight line with negative gradient. Since $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$, the gradient equals $-\Delta S^{\ominus}$. A falling line means $-\Delta S^{\ominus}$ is negative, so $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ is positive.

Explain the temperature effect**
With positive $\Delta S^{\ominus}$, the term $T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ grows more positive as $T$ increases from $350$ to $550$ $\text{K}$. Subtracting a larger positive number makes $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ less positive, eventually reaching zero at $550$ $\text{K}$.
Final answer: As $T$ increases, $T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ becomes more positive / $-T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ becomes more negative, so $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ decreases.
